questions.stem: A SaaS company gives each enterprise tenant a dedicated stack of resources in a shared AWS account, and every stack is created by the same CloudFormation template. Finance wants to see each tenant's monthly AWS cost, and the account managers want an email when any single tenant's month-to-date spend passes its contract allowance. Which combination of steps meets these requirements? (Choose two.)

options.text: Tag every resource in the stacks with a `tenant` tag in the template and activate it as a cost allocation tag in the Billing console.
options.why: Once activated, user-defined cost allocation tags appear in Cost Explorer and the Cost and Usage Report, so costs can be grouped by tenant.

options.text: Create an AWS Budgets cost budget for each tenant, filtered on the `tenant` tag, with email alerts at the allowance.
options.why: Budgets can filter on cost allocation tags and notify when actual or forecast spend crosses a threshold.

options.text: Create CloudWatch billing alarms on `EstimatedCharges` per tenant.
options.why: Billing metrics break down by service and linked account, not by tag, so there's no per-tenant alarm.

options.text: Use AWS Trusted Advisor cost checks for each tenant.
options.why: Trusted Advisor flags idle or under-used resources across the account; it doesn't report cost per tenant.

options.text: Move every tenant to its own AWS account under AWS Organizations this week.
options.why: Account-per-tenant gives clean cost separation, but it's a large migration and more than reporting needs, given that the stacks are already tagged by one template.

questions.explain: Cost visibility starts with tags: define them in templates, activate them as cost allocation tags (they are only tracked from activation onwards), then report in Cost Explorer or CUR and alert with Budgets. Shared pooled resources need metering instead, because tags can't split them.

questions.stem: A SaaS company serves enterprise customers in North America, Europe and Asia from one Region, and customers complain that settings changes made in their region of the world are slow to save. The settings data lives in Amazon DynamoDB. The company wants each geography to read and write locally, and the application must keep working in the other Regions if one Region fails. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Add DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX) clusters in each geography.
options.why: DAX caches reads in the same Region as the table. It doesn't make writes local and doesn't add Regional failover.

options.text: Use DynamoDB global tables with replicas in three Regions, and route each user to the nearest Region.
options.why: Global tables replicate in several Regions, so each Region can read and write locally, and the other Regions keep serving if one fails.

options.text: Export the table to Amazon S3 every hour and import it into tables in the other Regions.
options.why: Hourly copies are stale and read-only in practice. Writes made in other Regions would be lost or conflict.

options.text: Use DynamoDB Streams with a Lambda function that writes changes to tables in the other Regions.
options.why: This is a hand-built version of global tables, which you would have to operate yourself, including conflict handling and retries.

questions.explain: DynamoDB global tables give multi-Region, active-active tables without replication code. For multi-Region writes on DynamoDB, use global tables; on Aurora, global databases have one writer Region with fast failover.

questions.stem: A design-collaboration SaaS stores customer uploads in a single S3 bucket in us-east-1. Customers in Australia and India upload files of 2 GB to 10 GB over the internet, and uploads are slow and often restart. The company wants faster, more reliable uploads without adding Regions or servers. Which solution meets these requirements? (Choose two.)

options.text: Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration on the bucket and have clients use the accelerate endpoint.
options.why: Uploads enter the nearest edge location and travel over the AWS network to the bucket, which helps most with large files over long distances.

options.text: Use multipart upload in the clients so that parts upload in parallel and failed parts retry on their own.
options.why: Multipart uploads add parallelism and mean a failure only retries one part instead of the whole multi-GB file.

options.text: Put a CloudFront distribution in front of the bucket with caching enabled for PUT requests.
options.why: CloudFront doesn't cache uploads; caching applies to reads.

options.text: Change the bucket's storage class to S3 Express One Zone.
options.why: Express One Zone is for low-latency access from compute in the same AZ. It doesn't help long-distance internet uploads.

options.text: Create a Site-to-Site VPN from each customer office to us-east-1.
options.why: A VPN still goes over the internet, and setting it up for every customer is not practical for a SaaS product.

questions.explain: For large uploads from far away to one bucket, use multipart upload (parallel parts, retry per part) together with Transfer Acceleration (edge entry, AWS network). Use CloudFront for downloads. Both upload techniques are client-side changes, not infrastructure.

questions.stem: A SaaS company with 60 accounts in AWS Organizations must prove to auditors that every API call in every account, including accounts created in the future, is recorded. Logs must be stored centrally, and nobody in a member account, nor anyone who later gains access to the log bucket, may delete or overwrite them for seven years. Which combination of steps meets these requirements? (Choose two.)

options.text: Create an organization trail in CloudTrail from the management account so that it applies to all current and future member accounts.
options.why: An organization trail logs every account automatically, and member accounts can see it but cannot stop or change it.

options.text: Deliver the trail to an S3 bucket in a dedicated log archive account with S3 Object Lock in compliance mode and a seven-year retention.
options.why: A separate account removes member-account access to the bucket, and compliance-mode Object Lock stops anyone, including root, from deleting the logs early.

options.text: Ask each account owner to create a trail and enable log file validation.
options.why: Per-account trails depend on owners remembering new accounts, and owners can stop their own trails. Validation detects tampering but doesn't prevent deletion.

options.text: Send CloudTrail events to CloudWatch Logs in each account with a seven-year retention setting.
options.why: Retention settings set when logs expire, but anyone with permission in the account can still delete the log group.

options.text: Enable S3 Versioning with a lifecycle rule that expires noncurrent versions after seven years.
options.why: Versioning keeps overwritten objects, but a privileged user can still delete versions or change the lifecycle rule.

questions.explain: Audit logging at organization scale has two parts: collect with an organization trail, and protect in a separate log archive account with WORM storage (Object Lock compliance mode). AWS Control Tower sets up this layout by default.

questions.stem: A SaaS document platform stores tenant files in an S3 bucket in us-east-1. A new DR requirement says that a copy must exist in us-west-2, and that 99.9% of new objects must reach that copy within 15 minutes, backed by an SLA and with replication metrics to prove it. Which combination of steps meets these requirements? (Choose two.)

options.text: Enable S3 Versioning on both the source and destination buckets.
options.why: S3 Replication requires versioning on both the source and destination buckets.

options.text: Configure Cross-Region Replication with S3 Replication Time Control enabled.
options.why: Replication Time Control is designed to replicate 99.9% of objects within 15 minutes, comes with an SLA and turns on replication metrics.

options.text: Schedule an AWS DataSync task every 10 minutes to copy new objects to us-west-2.
options.why: DataSync can copy between buckets, but a schedule gives no per-object guarantee and no SLA for the 15-minute target.

options.text: Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration on the source bucket.
options.why: Transfer Acceleration speeds up client uploads over long distances; it doesn't replicate data between Regions.

options.text: Use S3 Batch Replication every 15 minutes.
options.why: Batch Replication is for existing objects and backfills, and running it on a timer doesn't give a time-bound guarantee for new objects.

questions.explain: S3 Replication needs versioning on both buckets. Add Replication Time Control when a requirement names a time bound or an SLA, and Batch Replication to copy objects that existed before the rule. Plan for deletes too: deletes are not replicated by default.

questions.stem: A company moved its engineering department's shared file system to Amazon EFS with 60 TB of data. Monitoring shows that about 80% of files are not read after their first month, but any file may be opened again unpredictably and must open without a restore step. Which change lowers storage cost the MOST with the LEAST effort?

options.text: Configure EFS lifecycle management to move files to Infrequent Access after 30 days without access, and back to Standard on first access.
options.why: EFS lifecycle policies move cold files to the much cheaper IA storage class automatically, and files stay in the same file system and path without a restore step.

options.text: Copy files older than 30 days to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval with a nightly script, delete them from EFS, and leave a stub file pointing to each archived copy.
options.why: This is cheaper to store, but opening a file would need a restore from S3, which breaks the no-restore requirement.

options.text: Move the file system to EBS volumes attached to an NFS server on EC2.
options.why: This adds a server to run and doesn't automatically move cold data to cheaper storage.

options.text: Switch the file system to Provisioned Throughput mode.
options.why: Throughput mode affects performance and its price, not storage cost.

questions.explain: EFS storage classes (Standard, Infrequent Access, Archive) with lifecycle management work like S3 lifecycle rules for file systems: cold files get cheaper while staying in the same path. Turn on the move back to Standard on first access when files can become active again.

questions.stem: A company migrating a customer portal to AWS will serve it through an Application Load Balancer at portal.example.com. The current certificates are renewed by hand every year, and an expired certificate caused a two-hour outage last spring. The company wants HTTPS with no manual renewal work. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Buy a certificate from a third-party authority, import it into AWS Certificate Manager, and attach it to the ALB.
options.why: ACM serves imported certificates, but it doesn't renew them. The yearly manual renewal and its outage risk stay.

options.text: Request a public certificate from AWS Certificate Manager with DNS validation and attach it to the ALB's HTTPS listener.
options.why: ACM public certificates are free and renew automatically while the DNS validation record stays in place, and the ALB picks up the renewed certificate.

options.text: Install the certificate on each EC2 instance and switch the ALB listener to TCP passthrough.
options.why: ALBs don't do TCP passthrough (that's an NLB feature), and certificates on every instance multiply the renewal work.

options.text: Use Let's Encrypt with a cron job on each instance to renew certificates every 60 days.
options.why: Automated, but the team owns the cron job on every instance, and it still terminates TLS on the instances instead of the ALB.

questions.explain: For ALB, CloudFront and API Gateway, use ACM public certificates with DNS validation: they are free and renew themselves. Imported certificates are never renewed by ACM, so treat an imported certificate as a manual task and monitor its expiry date.

questions.stem: A B2B scheduling SaaS migrated its booking API to AWS Lambda behind API Gateway. Most requests complete in 80 ms, but after quiet periods some take more than 2 seconds because of initialization, and enterprise customers' SLA requires p99 latency under 300 ms during business hours. Which solution meets the SLA MOST reliably?

options.text: Increase the function's memory to the maximum.
options.why: More memory speeds up initialization somewhat, but cold starts still happen, so the p99 target can still be missed.

options.text: Set reserved concurrency to the expected peak.
options.why: Reserved concurrency guarantees a capacity limit but doesn't pre-initialise execution environments.

options.text: Invoke the function every five minutes from an EventBridge schedule to keep it warm.
options.why: A ping keeps one or a few environments warm, but concurrent requests during spikes still need new environments, and this is a fragile workaround.

options.text: Configure provisioned concurrency on a function alias, scheduled with Application Auto Scaling for business hours.
options.why: Provisioned concurrency keeps initialised environments ready, so requests skip initialisation. Scheduling it for business hours limits the cost.

questions.explain: Provisioned concurrency is the managed answer to Lambda cold starts with a latency SLA; schedule it or scale it on utilisation to control cost. Reserved concurrency is a different control: it caps or guarantees capacity but doesn't keep environments warm.

questions.stem: A SaaS company offers its public REST API on Amazon API Gateway. One free-tier tenant's runaway script recently sent 4,000 requests per second, which pushed the backend database to its limits and slowed every other tenant. The company wants per-tenant request rates and monthly quotas that differ by pricing plan, enforced before requests reach the backend. What should the solutions architect configure?

options.text: API Gateway usage plans per pricing plan, with an API key for each tenant that is associated with its plan.
options.why: Usage plans apply throttling rates and quotas per API key, so each tenant is limited at the gateway according to its plan before requests reach the backend.

options.text: A higher account-level throttling limit for API Gateway in the Region.
options.why: The account limit applies to all tenants together. Raising it lets the noisy tenant use even more of the shared backend.

options.text: An Amazon CloudFront distribution in front of the API with caching enabled.
options.why: Caching helps for repeated GET requests, but it doesn't limit how many requests one tenant can send.

options.text: Reserved concurrency on the backend Lambda functions, sized so the database can handle the maximum number of concurrent requests.
options.why: This caps the backend for everyone together, so the noisy tenant can still use up the shared capacity and other tenants get throttled.

questions.explain: Noisy neighbours are a resilience problem in multi-tenant systems: enforce per-tenant limits at the edge. API Gateway usage plans and API keys are for metering and throttling, not for authentication; pair them with a real authorizer such as Cognito, IAM or a Lambda authorizer.

questions.stem: A SaaS company lets each product team create IAM roles for its own Lambda functions so that new tenant features ship without waiting for the security team. The security team must make sure that no role a developer creates can ever have more than read and write access to the team's own DynamoDB tables and S3 prefix, even if the developer attaches AdministratorAccess. Which approach meets these requirements?

options.text: Require developers to create roles from a CloudFormation template that the security team reviews.
options.why: Reviews catch mistakes but don't prevent them. Nothing stops a developer from attaching broader policies after deployment.

options.text: Use AWS Config rules with automatic remediation that deletes any role with the AdministratorAccess managed policy attached within a few minutes of its creation.
options.why: A detective control only fixes the problem after a powerful role already exists, and it only covers the one policy name it checks for.

options.text: Allow developers `iam:CreateRole` only if the role has a specific permissions boundary attached, and set that boundary to the team's tables and prefix.
options.why: The effective permissions of a role are the overlap of its policies and its boundary, so even AdministratorAccess can't go beyond the boundary. A condition on `iam:PermissionsBoundary` makes the boundary mandatory.

options.text: Attach an SCP to the developers' account that denies all DynamoDB and S3 actions.
options.why: This would block the features the teams are building. SCPs set account-wide limits; they don't scope individual roles to team resources.

questions.explain: Permissions boundaries are the safe way to delegate role creation: developers can create and change roles, but nothing they create can exceed the boundary. Make the boundary mandatory with the `iam:PermissionsBoundary` condition key, and deny changes to the boundary itself.

questions.stem: A migrated SaaS platform runs 1,200 gp2 EBS volumes of 1 TB each. Most volumes need about 3,000 IOPS and 125 MiB/s, but gp2 ties performance to volume size, so several databases were over-sized to 4 TB just to get IOPS. Which change reduces EBS cost the MOST without reducing performance?

options.text: Move all volumes to io2 with Elastic Volumes and provision exactly 3,000 IOPS on each, so that performance no longer depends on the volume size.
options.why: io2 provides highly durable provisioned IOPS, but it costs much more per GB and per IOPS than these workloads need.

options.text: Move the volumes to st1 throughput-optimised HDD.
options.why: st1 is cheap per GB but designed for large sequential reads, and random-access database workloads would slow down badly.

options.text: Take snapshots and recreate the volumes from them every month to compact them.
options.why: This doesn't change the price or volume type, and it disrupts workloads.

options.text: Change the volumes to gp3, which includes 3,000 IOPS and 125 MiB/s at any size, and move the oversized database volumes to smaller gp3 volumes.
options.why: gp3 costs less per GB than gp2 and includes a 3,000 IOPS and 125 MiB/s baseline at any size, so the oversized volumes no longer need extra capacity just for performance.

questions.explain: gp3 separates performance from size: baseline IOPS and throughput are included, and more can be bought separately. Moving from gp2 to gp3 is usually an online change with Elastic Volumes. Note that volumes can't be shrunk in place, so reclaiming oversized capacity requires a data copy.

questions.stem: A B2B time-tracking SaaS runs its web tier in an EC2 Auto Scaling group with target tracking on CPU. Every weekday at 08:30 in each customer time zone, logins jump fivefold within minutes, and new instances take seven minutes to become ready, so users see errors for the first ten minutes. The pattern has repeated for months. What is the MOST effective way to remove the errors?

options.text: Add predictive scaling to the Auto Scaling group so it launches capacity ahead of the daily peaks it has learned.
options.why: Predictive scaling forecasts the recurring daily pattern from history and launches instances before the peak, so the seven-minute warm-up happens in advance.

options.text: Lower the target CPU utilization of the target tracking policy from 60% to 30% so that the group scales out earlier when logins begin.
options.why: This keeps more headroom all day, which costs more, and the spike still outruns scaling.

options.text: Switch to a step scaling policy with larger steps.
options.why: Step scaling still reacts after the alarm fires, so the seven-minute delay remains.

options.text: Increase the health check grace period to 10 minutes.
options.why: This stops the group from replacing instances that are still starting, but doesn't add capacity any sooner.

questions.explain: Reactive scaling can't beat a launch time that is longer than the spike's ramp. For recurring, predictable peaks use predictive scaling or scheduled actions, and keep target tracking for the unexpected. Warm pools also shorten launch time when initialisation is slow.

questions.stem: A company is migrating an on-premises Java order system that uses Apache ActiveMQ through the JMS API and STOMP. The migration must be finished this quarter, the application team cannot rewrite the messaging code, and the broker must keep running if an Availability Zone fails. Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Rewrite the messaging code to use Amazon SQS with the SQS SDK.
options.why: SQS would eventually remove the broker, but the team can't rewrite the messaging code this quarter.

options.text: Install ActiveMQ on two EC2 instances in different AZs with a shared EFS directory.
options.why: This works, but the team would patch, monitor and fail over the broker itself.

options.text: Use Amazon MQ for ActiveMQ with an active/standby broker deployment across two AZs.
options.why: Amazon MQ runs ActiveMQ with the same JMS and STOMP protocols, so the code doesn't change, and the active/standby deployment fails over automatically across AZs.

options.text: Use Amazon MSK and point the application at the Kafka bootstrap servers.
options.why: Kafka uses its own protocol, so JMS and STOMP clients would have to be rewritten.

questions.explain: During a migration, protocol compatibility drives the choice: existing JMS, AMQP, MQTT, STOMP or OpenWire clients move to Amazon MQ unchanged. New cloud-native designs usually use SQS, SNS or EventBridge. A lift-and-shift that rewrites the code is no longer a lift-and-shift.

questions.stem: During migration, a company moved its on-premises PostgreSQL database to an Amazon RDS for PostgreSQL DB instance that was created without encryption. A customer audit now requires encryption at rest with an AWS KMS key, and a maintenance window of up to 30 minutes is allowed. Which combination of steps meets this requirement? (Choose two.)

options.text: Modify the existing DB instance and turn on storage encryption.
options.why: Tempting, but RDS can't encrypt an existing unencrypted DB instance in place. Encryption is fixed when the instance is created.

options.text: Take a snapshot of the instance and copy the snapshot with encryption enabled using the KMS key.
options.why: Copying a snapshot is the step where RDS lets you add encryption to unencrypted data.

options.text: Restore a new DB instance from the encrypted snapshot and point the application at it.
options.why: An instance restored from an encrypted snapshot is encrypted. Switching the endpoint over completes the move.

options.text: Create an encrypted read replica of the instance and promote it.
options.why: RDS doesn't let you create an encrypted read replica from an unencrypted instance.

options.text: Require SSL connections by setting `rds.force_ssl` to 1 in the parameter group.
options.why: This encrypts data in transit, which is good practice but doesn't meet the encryption-at-rest requirement.

questions.explain: Encryption at rest on RDS and EBS is chosen at creation. To encrypt existing data: snapshot it, copy the snapshot with encryption, restore from the copy, then switch over. Turn encryption on at creation for every new database so you never have to do this migration.

questions.stem: A SaaS e-learning company serves 45 TB per month of course videos and downloads directly from an S3 bucket to customers around the world. Data transfer out from S3 is now the largest line on the bill, and many popular files are downloaded thousands of times. Which change will reduce the data transfer cost the MOST while also improving download speed?

options.text: Enable S3 Transfer Acceleration on the bucket.
options.why: Transfer Acceleration speeds up transfers but adds a per-GB fee on top of normal data transfer, which raises the bill.

options.text: Serve the files through an Amazon CloudFront distribution with origin access control to the bucket.
options.why: Data transfer from S3 to CloudFront is free, popular files are served from edge caches, and CloudFront's data transfer price to the internet is generally lower than S3's.

options.text: Use S3 Cross-Region Replication to copy the bucket to three more Regions.
options.why: This multiplies storage and replication transfer charges, and every Region still pays data transfer out to users.

options.text: Use S3 Requester Pays on the bucket.
options.why: Requester Pays only works when requesters are authenticated AWS accounts, so it doesn't apply to public customers.

questions.explain: For repeated downloads to many users, put CloudFront in front of S3: origin-to-edge transfer is free, the cache absorbs repeat requests, and edge delivery is faster. Origin access control keeps the bucket private, so users can't bypass the CDN.

questions.stem: A company is moving a SaaS application's 3 TB on-premises Oracle database to Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL to remove licence costs. The database has stored procedures, the business allows less than one hour of downtime for the cutover, and the source must keep taking writes during the migration. Which combination of steps should the solutions architect use? (Choose two.)

options.text: Convert the schema, stored procedures and code with AWS Schema Conversion Tool or DMS Schema Conversion.
options.why: A heterogeneous move needs schema and code conversion first; these tools convert most objects automatically and flag what needs manual work.

options.text: Use AWS DMS with a full load followed by ongoing change data capture, and cut over once replication catches up.
options.why: Full load plus CDC keeps the target in sync while the source keeps taking writes, so downtime is only the short final switch.

options.text: Use AWS Application Migration Service to replicate the Oracle server to EC2.
options.why: This rehosts Oracle on EC2, keeping the licence costs the company wants to remove, and doesn't convert it to PostgreSQL.

options.text: Export the database with Oracle Data Pump and import the dump into Aurora PostgreSQL.
options.why: Data Pump dumps are Oracle's own format, and an offline export and import of 3 TB would exceed the downtime window.

options.text: Use AWS DataSync to copy the Oracle data files to Amazon EFS and attach them to Aurora.
options.why: Aurora can't use another engine's data files, and copying files from a running database doesn't produce a consistent copy.

questions.explain: Heterogeneous database migration has two parts: schema conversion (SCT or DMS Schema Conversion) and data movement (DMS full load plus CDC). CDC is what turns a long migration into a short cutover window. For a homogeneous move, use native tools or DMS without conversion.

questions.stem: A migrated SaaS application runs on EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group behind an Application Load Balancer. Twice this week, the Java process on an instance hung. The ALB stopped sending traffic to it, but the Auto Scaling group did not replace it for hours, and capacity stayed reduced. What should the solutions architect change so that unhealthy instances are replaced automatically?

options.text: Turn on Elastic Load Balancing health checks for the Auto Scaling group so it uses the target group's health check results.
options.why: By default, Auto Scaling only uses EC2 status checks, which pass while the operating system is up. With ELB health checks on, an instance that fails the application check is replaced.

options.text: Add a CloudWatch alarm on CPU utilization with a step scaling policy that scales out the group when average CPU stays above 70% for five minutes.
options.why: Scaling out adds capacity but leaves the hung instance in place, and a hung process may not even use much CPU.

options.text: Enable detailed monitoring on the instances.
options.why: One-minute metrics improve visibility but don't change how the group decides an instance is unhealthy.

options.text: Lower the target group's deregistration delay to 10 seconds.
options.why: This only shortens connection draining when targets are removed; it doesn't trigger replacement.

questions.explain: Auto Scaling replaces what it considers unhealthy. EC2 status checks see the hardware and operating system, while ELB health checks see the application. For web tiers behind a load balancer, turn on ELB health checks and choose a health check path that really exercises the application.

questions.stem: A SaaS company runs tenant workloads in containers that may execute customer-supplied scripts. Security requires that outbound traffic from these subnets reaches only about 20 allowed partner domains, such as `api.partner-billing.com`, over HTTPS. Partner IP addresses change often and without notice. Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Use security group egress rules that allow port 443 to the partners' current IP addresses.
options.why: Security groups only understand IP addresses and ports, and the partners' IPs change without notice, so the rules would always be out of date.

options.text: Use network ACLs that deny outbound traffic except to the partner CIDR blocks.
options.why: Same problem as IP-based security groups, plus NACLs are stateless and limited in rule count.

options.text: Route outbound traffic through a NAT gateway, enable VPC Flow Logs, and alert the security team when traffic goes to destinations outside the partners' ranges.
options.why: Flow Logs record traffic after it happens and can't block it. A NAT gateway on its own doesn't filter destinations.

options.text: Route outbound traffic through AWS Network Firewall with a stateful domain list rule group that allows only the partner domains.
options.why: Network Firewall's domain list rules check the TLS SNI or HTTP Host header and allow only the listed domains, whatever IP addresses they resolve to.

questions.explain: Security groups and NACLs filter by IP and port. To allow outbound traffic by domain name, use AWS Network Firewall (stateful domain lists) placed in the route between the workload subnets and the NAT or internet gateway. Firewall Manager can push the same policy across accounts.
